chapters.title: Chapter 7: Sector Rotation and Applying Sector Analysis

lessons.title: Building a Sector Scorecard on Screener.in

body.text: Everything you have learned in this course becomes useful only when it turns into a habit you repeat every quarter. A sector scorecard is that habit: one page per sector, the same columns every time, filled in after results season. It takes an hour to build and twenty minutes to update, and it stops you from judging a company by whichever number a headline happened to mention.

children.text: This lesson is practical. You will build a reusable scorecard using Screener.in, the free tool most Indian retail investors already use, plus company investor presentations for the sector-specific numbers Screener does not carry. By the end you will have a template you can apply to any sector covered in this course.

Open any company in the sector on Screener.in and use the classification links in its peer comparison section to see every listed company in the same industry, as you learned in Chapter 1. Click down to the most specific level that still leaves you four to eight meaningful peers, then remove companies whose business mix does not match. Keep the list small enough that you will actually maintain it. Eight companies is plenty; twenty is a spreadsheet you will abandon by the next quarter.

cells: Sales growth over 3 and 5 years, profit growth over 3 and 5 years
Operating profit margin, ROCE, ROE, and the 10-year range of margins
Screener annual profit and loss and ratios
Debt to equity, interest coverage, cash conversion or operating cash flow versus profit
Screener balance sheet and cash flow tables
P/E, price to book, dividend yield, and for cyclicals a normalised P/E you calculate yourself
The one or two numbers that actually run this industry
Company investor presentations and earnings calls
Where you think the sector sits in its cycle, and what would change your mind

body.text: Screener's standard columns are built for manufacturing and services companies. For banks, NBFCs, and insurers, debt to equity, operating profit margin, and interest coverage are meaningless or misleading, as you saw in Chapter 3. For developers, reported revenue lags reality by years. Always swap in the right metrics for the business model before comparing anything.

children.text: Step 4: Compute the Two Numbers Screener Will Not Give You

Two calculations do most of the work in a scorecard, and both are easy once the data is in front of you. The first is the sector median for each valuation column, which gives you a benchmark to judge any single company against. The second is normalised P/E for cyclicals, from Chapter 2. If you are comfortable with a spreadsheet, a median formula is enough. If you prefer code, the snippet below does both.

body.caption: A small helper for sector medians and normalised P/E
body.code:
from statistics import median

# P/E of each company in your peer set
peer_pe = {
    "Company A": 18,
    "Company B": 22,
    "Company C": 25,
    "Company D": 31,
    "Company E": 44,
}

sector_median_pe = median(peer_pe.values())
print("Sector median P/E:", sector_median_pe)

for name, pe in peer_pe.items():
    premium = (pe / sector_median_pe - 1) * 100
    print(f"{name}: {premium:+.1f}% vs sector median")

# Normalised P/E for a cyclical: price divided by average EPS over a full cycle
price = 600
eps_history = [10, 40, 100, 30, 5]  # oldest to latest
normalised_eps = sum(eps_history) / len(eps_history)
print("Normalised EPS:", normalised_eps)
print("Normalised P/E:", round(price / normalised_eps, 1))

body.title: Find the Sector Median
body.prompt: Your peer set has P/E ratios of 18, 22, 25, 31, and 44. What is the sector median P/E?
body.explanation: Sorted, the middle value of 18, 22, 25, 31, 44 is 25. Use the median rather than the average here, because one extreme value, 44 in this case, would pull the average up to 28 and distort your benchmark. A company trading at 31 is then at a 24% premium to the sector median, and your job is to decide whether its growth, returns, or balance sheet justify that.

body.title: Which Column Should You Drop?
body.question: You are building a scorecard for private sector banks. Which column from the standard template is least useful and should be replaced?
body.explanation: Debt to equity is meaningless for a bank, because deposits and borrowings are its raw material rather than a risk measure, as you saw in Chapter 1. Replace it with capital adequacy, GNPA, and provision coverage. Return on assets, price to book, and loan growth all belong in a bank scorecard.

body.title: Useful Screener.in habits while building this

children.text: A few practices make the scorecard much faster to maintain. Save a screen with your preferred numeric filters so you can re-run it each quarter instead of rebuilding it. Use the export option on a company page to pull the annual profit and loss, balance sheet, and cash flow into a spreadsheet rather than retyping numbers. Add companies you track to a watchlist so you see them together. Use the notes feature, or your own document, to record why you rated each company the way you did, because in three months you will not remember.

Two cautions. First, standardised data can misclassify or lag, especially after mergers, demergers, or a change in reporting, so cross-check anything surprising against the company filing. Second, screens find candidates, they do not make decisions. Every shortlisted name still needs the sector-specific work you learned in this course.

body.title: Using the Scorecard to Make a Call
body.scenario: Your cement scorecard for five companies after results season shows: Company A at EBITDA per tonne of ₹1,250 with utilisation at 82% and net debt to EBITDA of 0.4, trading at an EV per tonne of ₹9,500 crore per million tonnes of capacity. Company B has EBITDA per tonne of ₹700, utilisation at 64%, net debt to EBITDA of 3.1, and trades at half A's EV per tonne. The sector median P/E is 32, A trades at 38 and B at 21. Industry utilisation is improving and few new plants are being announced.
body.prompt: What does the scorecard tell you, and what would you do next?
body.modelAnswer: The scorecard separates quality from price. Company A is the stronger operator: higher EBITDA per tonne, better utilisation, and a clean balance sheet, and the market is charging a premium for that on both P/E and EV per tonne. Company B is cheaper on every measure, but the cheapness has a reason: weak profitability per tonne, low utilisation, and leverage of 3.1 times EBITDA, which is dangerous in a cyclical business as you saw in Chapter 2. The sector context matters here: improving utilisation with little new capacity being announced points to a mid-cycle setup rather than a peak, which historically favours operating leverage. That is the case for B, since a rise in prices and utilisation would lift its margins from a low base far more than A's. But B only works if it survives its debt, so the next steps are specific: check B's interest coverage and debt maturities, whether its plants are in regions where prices are actually improving, its lead distance and fuel costs, and whether management is cutting capex to deleverage. If the balance sheet cannot handle another weak year, the higher quality company at a premium is the sounder choice. Note also that P/E is the weakest column on this scorecard for cement; normalised EV/EBITDA and EV per tonne carry more weight.

body.text: Update the scorecard on a schedule tied to the sector, not to the news. Most sectors need a refresh once a quarter after results. Autos deserve a monthly look at sales data, cement a check on regional prices, and metals a check on global benchmark prices. Everything else can wait for results season.

body.label: Screener.in
body.description: Build your peer set from the classification links on any company page, then use screens, watchlists, and the export option to maintain your scorecard each quarter.

body.title: Fill in the Blank
body.textWithBlank: When benchmarking a company's valuation against its peers, prefer the sector ___ rather than the average, because one extreme value can distort the average.
body.explanation: The median is the middle value, so an outlier at either end does not drag the benchmark away from where most of the sector trades.

body.title: Build Your First Sector Scorecard This Week
steps: Pick one sector you already own through stocks or funds
Build a peer set of four to eight comparable companies using Screener classification links
Create the standard columns: identity, growth, profitability, balance sheet, valuation
Replace any column that does not fit the business model, especially for lenders, insurers, and developers
Add the sector KPI columns from this course, filled in from the latest investor presentations
Calculate the sector median for each valuation column, and normalised P/E for cyclicals
Write one line on where the sector sits in its cycle and one line on what would change your view
Diarise the update for the week after next quarter's results

points: A sector scorecard is a repeatable one-page comparison: same peers, same columns, updated after every results season
Build the peer set from Screener classification links, then trim it to companies with genuinely comparable business models
Standard columns suit manufacturing and services; swap them out for lenders, insurers, and developers
Add the one or two KPIs that actually run the sector, which usually come from investor presentations rather than screeners
Calculate the sector median for valuation columns, and normalised P/E for cyclicals, because screeners show reported P/E
Record your judgement on where the sector sits in its cycle and what would change your mind, so you can check yourself later
Screens generate candidates; the sector-specific analysis from this course is what turns a candidate into a decision

body.text: Company names in the examples are hypothetical and all figures are illustrative. Screener.in features and data presentation can change; verify anything surprising against company filings on NSE, BSE, or the company website. Nothing here is investment advice or a recommendation to buy or sell any security.
